items.question_text: Assertion: Suppose reference frames S₁ and S₂ are both non-inertial; then an observer in S₁ would find S₂ to be an inertial frame. Reason: A frame being in motion does not by itself make it non-inertial.

options.label: (a)
options.text: both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion

options.label: (b)
options.text: both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion

options.label: (c)
options.text: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false

options.label: (d)
options.text: Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

solution.approach: Check whether the relative acceleration of S₂ with respect to S₁ must vanish merely because both are non-inertial, then judge the general truth of the Reason on its own.

steps.text: A frame is non-inertial only if it has some acceleration relative to an inertial (ground) frame; being non-inertial is about acceleration, not about motion in general.
Viewed from S₁, the relative acceleration of S₂ is the difference of their accelerations relative to the ground.
steps.equation: a(S₂ relative to S₁) = a(S₂) − a(S₁)

steps.text: This difference is zero only in the special case that S₁ and S₂ happen to share the same acceleration, which is not stated here, so in general S₂ stays non-inertial even when viewed from S₁ — the Assertion is false as a general claim.
steps.equation: a(S₂) − a(S₁) ≠ 0 in general ⇒ Assertion false

steps.text: The Reason is a true, separate statement: a frame moving at constant velocity is still inertial, so mere motion does not make a frame non-inertial — only acceleration does.
steps.equation: Assertion false, Reason true = both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion

final_answer.value: both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion

items.question_text: A 2 kg cube, 20 cm on each edge, is pressed flat against a rough vertical wall by a horizontal force F of 40 N that passes through the cube's centre, point C. Taking g = 10 m/s², find how far the wall's normal reaction acts from point C, measured perpendicular to F.
items.figure_description: A cube (drawn as a square in side view) is pressed against a vertical wall on its right-hand side by a horizontal force F applied at its left face, acting through the cube's centre C. The wall's surface is rough (frictional) and vertical.

solution.approach: Find the wall's normal force and the friction from equilibrium, then balance torques about C to find how far below C the wall's contact force must act.

steps.text: Since F passes through C and is horizontal, horizontal equilibrium gives the wall's normal reaction equal to F.
Vertical equilibrium requires friction from the wall to support the cube's weight.
Both F and the weight act through C, so they create no torque about C. The wall's normal force and friction act together at the contact point, a horizontal distance of half a side from C.
steps.equation: horizontal distance from C to wall face = 0.20/2 = 0.10 m

steps.text: Let the contact point be a distance h above C. Balance the torques of N and f about C.
Solve for h and take its magnitude as the perpendicular distance.
steps.equation: h = −(20×0.10)/40 = −0.05 m, so the distance is 0.05 m (below C)

final_answer.value: 0.05 m (5 cm), below the centre C

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting that F and the weight pass through C (so they cannot be left out of the torque count as if they contributed) leads to setting up the wrong torque equation.
Using the full side length instead of half the side for the horizontal distance from C to the wall face gives 0.10 m instead of 0.05 m.

items.question_text: Assertion: Suppose reference frames S₁ and S₂ are both non-inertial; then an observer in S₁ would find S₂ to be an inertial frame. Reason: A frame being in motion does not by itself make it non-inertial.

options.label: (a)
options.text: both Assertion and Reason are true and the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion

options.label: (b)
options.text: both Assertion and Reason are true but the Reason is not the correct explanation of the Assertion

options.label: (c)
options.text: Assertion is true, but the Reason is false

options.label: (d)
options.text: Assertion is false, but the Reason is true

solution.approach: Check whether the relative acceleration of S₂ with respect to S₁ must vanish merely because both are non-inertial, then judge the general truth of the Reason on its own.

steps.text: A frame is non-inertial only if it has some acceleration relative to an inertial (ground) frame; being non-inertial is about acceleration, not about motion in general.
Viewed from S₁, the relative acceleration of S₂ is the difference of their accelerations relative to the ground.
steps.equation: a(S₂ relative to S₁) = a(S₂) − a(S₁)

steps.text: This difference is zero only in the special case that S₁ and S₂ happen to share the same acceleration, which is not stated here, so in general S₂ stays non-inertial even when viewed from S₁ — the Assertion is false as a general claim.
steps.equation: a(S₂) − a(S₁) ≠ 0 in general ⇒ Assertion false

steps.text: The Reason is a true, separate statement: a frame moving at constant velocity is still inertial, so mere motion does not make a frame non-inertial — only acceleration does.

final_answer.value: If the Assertion is false but the Reason is true.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming that viewing one non-inertial frame from another non-inertial frame always cancels out the acceleration completely, making S₂ look inertial from S₁ in every case, and picking both statements true.

items.question_text: For the same pulley system, with block 1 hanging from the fixed pulley and blocks 2 and 3 hanging from the two ends of the movable pulley, block 3 accelerates downward at 6 m/s² and block 2 accelerates upward at 4 m/s². Determine the acceleration of block 1.
items.figure_description: A fixed pulley is mounted at the top, attached to a rigid support. A string runs over this fixed pulley: block 1 hangs from one end (the left side), and the other end connects to the axle of a second, movable pulley that hangs below it. A second string runs over this movable pulley, with block 2 hanging from its left end and block 3 hanging from its right end.

solution.approach: Use the movable-pulley constraint to find the pulley's acceleration from blocks 2 and 3, then use the fixed-pulley constraint to find block 1's acceleration.

steps.text: Take downward as positive. Block 3's acceleration is 6 m/s² downward and block 2's is 4 m/s² upward, so its downward value is −4 m/s².
The movable-pulley constraint makes the pulley's downward acceleration the average of the two.
The fixed-pulley constraint makes block 1's downward acceleration the negative of the movable pulley's.
A negative downward acceleration means block 1 actually accelerates upward.

common_mistakes.text: Taking block 1's acceleration in the same direction as the movable pulley instead of the opposite direction gives 1 m/s² downward, the wrong direction.

items.question_text: A frictionless pulley is fixed to a ceiling. A light string that does not stretch passes over it: a 2 kg block hangs from one end. From the other end the string leads down to a 4 kg block; a second light string then connects the 4 kg block to a 6 kg block hanging below it. Taking g = 10 m/s², find the acceleration of the system and the tension in each of the two strings.
items.figure_description: A single fixed pulley hangs from the ceiling. A string over the pulley holds a 2 kg block on one side, moving upward with acceleration a. On the other side, the string (tension T₁) runs down to a 4 kg block; a second string (tension T₂) hangs below the 4 kg block and connects it to a 6 kg block. The 4 kg and 6 kg blocks move downward together with acceleration a.

solution.approach: The 4 kg and 6 kg blocks move together as one 10 kg mass on the heavier side of the pulley, giving a plain two-mass pulley problem.

steps.text: The 2 kg block goes up and the combined 4 kg + 6 kg = 10 kg goes down with the same acceleration a.
Put in g = 10 m/s² and solve.
T₁ is the tension pulling the 2 kg block up, so apply Newton's second law to it.
Put in a = 20/3 m/s² and solve for T₁.
T₂ is the tension pulling the 6 kg block up from below the 4 kg block, so apply Newton's second law to the 6 kg block.
Put in a = 20/3 m/s² and solve for T₂.
steps.why_this_step: The 6 kg block feels only its own weight down and T₂ up, since nothing hangs below it.

common_mistakes.text: Forgetting the 4 kg block and taking the heavier side as only 6 kg, giving a = (6−2)×10/8 = 5 m/s².
Treating the 6 kg block as not accelerating and taking T₂ = 6g = 60 N.

items.question_text: A student claims that in a non-inertial (accelerating) reference frame, the only way to analyse a mechanics problem is by bringing in a pseudo force. Decide whether this claim is correct or incorrect.

solution.approach: A problem set in a non-inertial frame can also be solved by working entirely in an inertial frame with only real forces, so pseudo force is not the only method.

steps.text: Every non-inertial-frame problem can be solved by switching to an inertial, ground frame and using Newton's second law with only real forces, never needing a pseudo force at all.
Pseudo force is added only as a convenience, so that Newton's second law appears to hold when the calculation is done directly inside the accelerating frame.
Since the ground-frame method with real forces alone always works, the claim that pseudo force is the only way to solve such problems is false.

items.question_text: A straight rod AB lies inside a spherical shell whose inner surface is rough. The shell rests on the ground below it. The rod's two ends, A and B, touch this rough inner surface at two different points. Draw a diagram of the rod on its own, showing all the forces that act on it.
items.figure_description: A circle represents the cross-section of a spherical shell resting on a horizontal ground below it. A straight rod lies inside the circle as a chord, touching the shell's rough inner surface at two points: end A near the bottom-left of the circle, close to where the shell meets the ground, and end B on the right side of the circle, above the mid-height.

solution.approach: At each contact point the rough shell gives a normal force toward its centre and a friction force along its surface, plus the rod's own weight.

steps.text: Mark the weight of the rod, Mg, acting vertically downward at its midpoint.
steps.equation: Mg ↓ at the midpoint of AB

steps.text: At end A, mark the normal reaction Nₐ directed from A toward the centre of the shell, and a friction force fₐ tangent to the shell surface at A, since the shell is rough.
steps.equation: Nₐ toward centre, fₐ tangent, both at A

steps.text: At end B, mark the normal reaction N_B directed from B toward the centre of the shell, and a friction force f_B tangent to the shell surface at B.
steps.equation: N_B toward centre, f_B tangent, both at B

steps.text: The free body diagram of the rod carries five forces in total.
steps.equation: Mg at the midpoint; Nₐ and fₐ at A; N_B and f_B at B
steps.why_this_step: Each contact with a rough curved surface gives a normal part toward the centre and a friction part along the surface.

final_answer.value: Five forces act on the rod: weight Mg at its midpoint, normal reaction Nₐ and friction fₐ at A, and normal reaction N_B and friction f_B at B, each normal force pointing toward the shell's centre and each friction force along the shell surface.

common_mistakes.text: Drawing only a normal force at A and B and leaving out friction, forgetting that the shell is stated to be rough.
Directing the normal forces along the rod instead of toward the shell's centre; a normal force from a curved surface always acts along the radius.

items.question_text: A 4 kilogram block rests on a rough horizontal surface. A force that varies with time, F = kt, acts horizontally on it, where k = 2 N·s⁻¹. Given μ = 0.2, work out the friction acting between block and surface exactly when t = 2 s.

solution.approach: Find the applied force at t = 2 s and the maximum friction the surface can supply, then check that the applied force has not yet reached that maximum.

steps.text: Find the size of the applied force at t = 2 s.
Find the maximum friction force the surface can supply, using the normal force, which equals the block's weight on this horizontal plane.
Since the applied force, 4 N, is smaller than the maximum friction, 8 N, the block is still at rest, and friction matches the applied force to keep it still.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming friction is always at its maximum value once any force is applied, without checking whether the block has actually started moving, gives f = μmg = 8 N.

items.question_text: In the figure, three massless strings meet at a common knot. A horizontal string connects the knot to a fixed wall; the tension in this string is 30 N. A second string runs from the knot up to a fixed support, making a 45° angle with the vertical. A third string hangs straight down from the knot and supports a block of weight W. Find W.
items.figure_description: Three massless strings are tied together at one knot. A horizontal string runs from the knot to a fixed vertical wall. An inclined string runs from the same knot up to a fixed support, making a 45° angle with the vertical direction. A third string hangs straight down from the knot, with a block of weight W tied to its lower end.

solution.approach: At the knot, resolve the diagonal string's tension along the horizontal and vertical directions and balance each against the known tension and the hanging weight.

steps.text: At the knot, three strings pull: the diagonal string at 45° from the vertical, the horizontal string with tension 30 N, and the vertical string carrying weight W.
Balance the horizontal direction: the diagonal string's horizontal component equals the horizontal string's tension.
Solve for the diagonal string's tension T.
Balance the vertical direction: the diagonal string's vertical component supports the weight W.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the diagonal string's two components must differ since the string is drawn at an angle, missing that 45° makes sin45° equal cos45°, so W also equals 30 N.
Setting W equal to the full diagonal tension T = 30√2 N ≈ 42.4 N, instead of only its vertical component.

items.question_text: A rope, of mass M and length L, lies on a rough horizontal floor. A steady force drags it horizontally, with magnitude F = Mg, applied at one end and pointing along the rope's own length. Between rope and floor, the coefficient of kinetic friction is 1/2. Find the tension exactly at the rope's midpoint.

solution.approach: Find the rope's overall acceleration from the pull and the friction, then apply Newton's second law to the trailing half of the rope to find the tension at its midpoint.

steps.text: The whole rope has the pulling force F on one end and friction, spread evenly along its length, resisting the motion. Find the acceleration from the net force on the whole rope.
steps.equation: F − μMg = Ma, with F = Mg and μ = 1/2 ⇒ a = g(1 − μ) = g/2

steps.text: Look at the trailing half of the rope, the half farther from where F is pulled. The only forces on it are the tension T pulling it forward from the midpoint and friction on its own weight holding it back.
steps.equation: trailing half has mass M/2 and friction μ(M/2)g

steps.text: Apply Newton's second law to this half and solve for T.

common_mistakes.text: Wrongly assuming all the friction acts only under the far half of the rope, leaving none on the trailing half, gives T = (M/2)a = Mg/4.

items.question_text:
In the arrangement shown, take g = 10 m/s² and find (a) the accelerations of the 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg blocks, and (b) the tensions T₁ and T₂.
(a) the acceleration of each of the 1 kg, 2 kg and 3 kg blocks
(b) the tensions T₁ and T₂
items.figure_description: A 1 kg block rests on a smooth horizontal table. A string of tension T₂ runs from the block to the right, over a small pulley fixed at the table's edge, then straight down, passes UNDER a movable pulley P₁ (wrapping around its lower half) and rises vertically to a fixed anchor on the ceiling; P₁ therefore hangs in the loop of the T₂ string. From the axle of P₁ a short vertical string hangs down to the axle of a second movable pulley P₂ directly below it. A string of tension T₁ passes over P₂: a 2 kg block hangs from its left end and a 3 kg block from its right end. All pulleys and strings are light and frictionless. When the 1 kg block moves right by x, P₁ and P₂ descend by x/2.

solution.approach: Use the two given string constraints to relate all four accelerations, note the two movable pulleys make T1 equal T2, then solve the three block equations together.

steps.text: The 1 kg block's string loops under the movable pulley P1, so P1 (and P2, joined rigidly below it) descend at half the 1 kg block's speed; this is given directly: when the 1 kg block moves x, P1 and P2 descend x/2.
steps.why_this_step: This is the first constraint relation, fixed by the string geometry, written before any force equation.

steps.text: The 2 kg and 3 kg blocks hang from a string over the movable pulley P2, so their accelerations add up to twice P2's own acceleration.
steps.why_this_step: This is the second constraint relation, from treating P2 as an ordinary pulley that itself accelerates at aP.

steps.text: P1 is massless: the two upward pulls of the T2 cord (looped under it) must balance the one downward pull of the short link to P2, and P2 is massless too: that link's pull upward must balance the two downward pulls of the T1 cord.
Write Newton's second law for the 1 kg block on the frictionless table.
Write Newton's second law for the 2 kg and the 3 kg blocks, taking downward as positive.
steps.equation: m2 g − T1 = m2 a2,   m3 g − T1 = m3 a3

steps.text: Using T1 = T2 = 2m1 aP, express a2 and a3 in terms of aP, substitute into a2 + a3 = 2aP, and solve.
Use aP to find the remaining accelerations and the common tension.

final_answer.value: acceleration of 1 kg block = 120/11 ≈ 10.9 m/s²; of 2 kg block = 50/11 ≈ 4.5 m/s² downward; of 3 kg block = 70/11 ≈ 6.4 m/s² downward; T1 = T2 = 120/11 ≈ 10.9 N

common_mistakes.text: Treating P2 as fixed and solving the 2 kg-3 kg pair as an ordinary Atwood machine, giving accelerations of 2 m/s² each way instead of the correct 4.5 and 6.4 m/s².

items.question_text: A block of mass 2 kg sits on a rough horizontal floor whose friction coefficient is μ = 0.8. A horizontal force that grows with time, F = 2t newton (with t in seconds), pushes the block, as pictured. Using g = 10 m/s², sketch how the block's acceleration changes with time.
items.figure_description: A 2 kg block rests on a rough horizontal floor with friction coefficient μ = 0.8. A horizontal force F = 2t (F in newton, t in seconds) pushes the block to the right, increasing with time.

solution.approach: The block stays still until the growing force F = 2t exceeds the maximum friction, then it accelerates according to Newton's second law with that same friction opposing it.

steps.text: With only one μ given, the same value acts as both the static limit and the kinetic value once the block moves.
Find the time at which F first reaches this value; before that time the block does not move, so a = 0.
For t ≥ 8 s, the block slides, and kinetic friction (16 N, same value) opposes F; apply Newton's second law.
The full acceleration-time graph is flat at zero up to t = 8 s, then rises as a straight line of slope 1 starting from a = 0 at t = 8 s.
steps.equation: a = 0 for 0 ≤ t < 8 s; a = (t − 8) m/s² for t ≥ 8 s

final_answer.value: a = 0 for 0 ≤ t < 8 s; for t ≥ 8 s, a = (t − 8) m/s², a straight line starting at a = 0 when t = 8 s and rising with slope 1 m/s³ (no jump at t = 8 s, since the same μ gives the same friction immediately before and immediately after motion starts).

common_mistakes.text: Assuming motion starts at t = 0 and writing a = t − 8 for all t, giving a wrongly negative acceleration before t = 8 s.
Forgetting to subtract the friction force after motion starts and writing a = t (using F = 2t directly divided by mass without subtracting 16 N of friction).

items.question_text:
Three blocks with masses 4 kg, 2 kg and 1 kg, placed in that order, sit in a row on a frictionless surface. Two light strings that do not stretch join consecutive blocks — one between the 4 kg and 2 kg blocks, another between the 2 kg and 1 kg blocks. A horizontal pull of 14 N is applied to the 1 kg block, directed away from the other two blocks.
(a) Determine how fast each block accelerates.
(b) Determine the pulling force transmitted through each string.
items.figure_description: Three blocks lie in a row on a horizontal frictionless surface, left to right: 4 kg, then 2 kg, then 1 kg. A light inextensible string (tension T₂) connects the 4 kg and 2 kg blocks; another light inextensible string (tension T₁) connects the 2 kg and 1 kg blocks. A horizontal force of 14 N pulls the 1 kg block to the right, away from the other two blocks.

solution.approach: Find the common acceleration of the three-block system, then apply Newton's second law to each block in turn, starting from the pulled end, to find each string's tension.

steps.text: The pulling force F acts on the whole chain of three blocks through the strings, and the surface is smooth, so all three move with one common acceleration.
Look at the 1 kg block alone, the one being pulled. F acts forward on it, and T₁ (the string to the 2 kg block) pulls it back.
Look at the 4 kg block alone, the one farthest from the pull. Only T₂ (the string to the 2 kg block) acts on it, pulling it forward.
steps.why_this_step: The 4 kg block has no other horizontal force on it, so its whole forward force is the string tension pulling it along.

final_answer.value: (a) acceleration of each block = 2 m/s², (b) tension T₂ (between the 4 kg and 2 kg blocks) = 8 N, tension T₁ (between the 2 kg and 1 kg blocks) = 12 N

common_mistakes.text: Finding T₁ and T₂ as equal, missing that the string closer to the pulled block always carries more tension because it also has to move the blocks behind it.
Computing the acceleration using only the 1 kg block's mass, giving 14 m/s² instead of dividing by the total mass of the chain.

items.question_text: A knot is held in place by three strings. String C runs horizontally from the knot to a wall. String B runs from the knot up to the ceiling, making a 30° angle with the vertical. String A hangs vertically down from the knot and supports a block of mass 10 kg. The whole system is in equilibrium. Which string has zero tension?
items.figure_description: A vertical wall on the left and a horizontal ceiling meet at a corner. From a common knot below and to the right of the corner, string C runs horizontally to the left to the wall, string B runs up and to the right to the ceiling making a 30° angle with the vertical dashed line through the knot (so 60° with the ceiling), and string A hangs straight down from the knot, holding a 10 kg block at its bottom end.

solution.approach: Balance the knot vertically and horizontally to find all three string tensions, then check whether any of them actually comes out zero.

steps.text: At the knot, three strings pull: A straight down carrying the 10 kg block, B up along 30° to the ceiling, and C straight toward the wall (horizontal).
Balance the vertical direction; only T(A) and the vertical part of T(B) act vertically.
Solve for T(B).
Balance the horizontal direction; only T(C) and the horizontal part of T(B) act horizontally.
All three tensions come out clearly positive, so none of the strings carries zero tension.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming a horizontal string like C carries no load since it does not hold up any weight directly, missing that it must balance the horizontal pull of the angled string B.

items.question_text: Two blocks are in contact with each other and are sliding down an incline that makes 30° with the horizontal. Between the 2.0 kg block and the incline surface, the friction coefficient is μ₁ = 0.20; between the 4.0 kg block and the incline surface, it is μ₂ = 0.30. The 2.0 kg block sits higher up the slope, pressing against the 4.0 kg block, which sits lower down. Using g = 10 m/s², work out the acceleration of the 2.0 kg block.
items.figure_description: Two blocks touch each other on an incline of 30° to the horizontal: the 2.0 kg block sits higher up the slope, in contact with the 4.0 kg block which sits lower down; both slide down together.

solution.approach: The two blocks touch and slide down together with a common acceleration, so treat them as one system of total mass 6 kg with each block contributing its own friction.

steps.text: Write the weight component along the incline and the friction force for the combined system, using each block's own friction coefficient.
Substitute the given values: m₁ = 2.0 kg, μ₁ = 0.20, m₂ = 4.0 kg, μ₂ = 0.30, θ = 30°, g = 10 m/s².
Solve for the common acceleration.
steps.why_this_step: Since μ₂ > μ₁, the 4.0 kg block in front resists more, so the 2.0 kg block behind pushes into it; this contact force does not change the combined system's acceleration because it is internal to the system.

final_answer.value: a ≈ 2.69 m/s², directed down the incline

common_mistakes.text: Using only the 2.0 kg block's own friction coefficient (0.20) for the whole system gives a ≈ 3.27 m/s², ignoring that the two blocks are pressed together and share the load.
Using only the 4.0 kg block's friction coefficient (0.30) for the whole system gives a ≈ 2.40 m/s², again ignoring that each block contributes its own friction.

items.question_text: A 2 kg block and a 4 kg block sit touching each other on a smooth incline that makes an angle of 30° with the horizontal; the 4 kg block is lower down the slope and the 2 kg block is higher up, in contact with it. Both blocks are let go from rest at the same instant. Find the normal force that acts between the two blocks.
items.figure_description: A wedge shaped like a right triangle has its sloped face rising at 30° from the horizontal, the angle marked where the slope meets the base. Two blocks touch each other on this sloped face, tilted to match the slope: a 4 kg block positioned lower down the slope, and a 2 kg block positioned higher up the slope, right above it.

solution.approach: With no applied force besides gravity and a frictionless incline, both blocks would accelerate at the same rate on their own, so they need no push from each other.

steps.text: On a smooth incline with no applied force, a block's acceleration along the slope depends only on gravity and the incline angle, not on its mass.
steps.equation: a = g sin30°, the same value for both blocks

steps.text: Since both blocks would accelerate at the same rate even if they were separate, neither block needs to push on the other to keep pace.
The normal contact force between the two blocks is therefore zero.

common_mistakes.text: Assuming the heavier 4 kg block pushes on the lighter 2 kg block because it sits lower on the slope, missing that acceleration on a smooth incline does not depend on mass.
Computing a contact force from the mass difference, such as (4−2)g sin30° = 10 N, a method that only applies when an outside force acts on the pair.
